questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.stem: Which revision fixes the comma splice in the memo sentence?

The plan was approved, the council funded it.

questions.explanation: A definition-first introduction states the term's meaning before the claim; vague or delayed versions fail.

Traffic fell sharply, and the lane closed.

questions.stem: Explain why a dangling modifier confuses readers.

answer.exemplar: A dangling modifier attaches to the wrong noun, so readers picture the wrong actor performing the action described in the sentence.

questions.stem: Explain when a fragment can work as a stylistic choice.

answer.exemplar: A fragment works when it is purposeful and brief, adding emphasis or rhythm, rather than accidental or unclear to the sentence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.stem: Explain why a comma splice is a grammatical error.

answer.exemplar: A comma splice joins two independent clauses with only a comma, which cannot coordinate clauses on its own in standard English.

questions.explanation: A comma alone cannot join independent clauses; use a conjunction or semicolon.

questions.stem: Explain why an introduction should begin with a definition.

answer.exemplar: Beginning with a definition establishes shared meaning, so readers understand the term before evaluating the claim in the memo.

questions.explanation: Shared meaning first prevents confusion; claims land better after it.

questions.explanation: Cause-first order sets up the result; reversed order obscures it.

questions.stem: Explain why a counterargument strengthens a memo.

answer.exemplar: A counterargument shows fairness and lets the writer rebut the strongest opposing view, improving credibility with readers.

questions.explanation: Fairness plus rebuttal builds trust; ignoring opposition weakens it.

questions.explanation: Over-concession abandons the argument; concede then pivot.

questions.stem: Explain why a conclusion should not merely summarize.
